In this paper, we investigate the properties of the three millimeter galaxies hosting X-ray detected AGNs in the ALCS, using the archival data of *Chandra*.

We estimate the X-ray luminosities (or mass-accretion rates), star-formation rates, and stellar masses of this sample, and discuss their evolutional stages in comparison with other X-ray detected samples.

Utilizing the archival data of *Chandra*, we identify three AGNs at $z=$1.06, 2.09, and 2.84 among the 180 millimeter sources securely detected in the ALCS (of which 155 are inside the coverage of *Chandra*).

The X-ray spectral analysis shows that two AGNs are not significantly absorbed ($\log N_{\mathrm{H}}/\mathrm{cm}^{-2} < 23$), while the other shows signs of moderate absorption ($\log N_{\mathrm{H}}/\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\sim 23.5$).
The SED analysis suggests that A370-ID110 is a type 2 AGN, whereas M0416-ID117 and M0329-ID11 are type 1 AGNs.

We find that all the sources are classified as ultra-luminous infrared galaxies ($L_{\mathrm{IR}}/L_{\odot} > 10^{12}$) and show high star-formation rates ($\mathrm{SFR}\gtrsim 100\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$).

Our sample is distributed close to the main sequence lines (within 0.2 dex along the SFR axis). This indicates that our sources are normal star-forming galaxies at $z$=1–3, i.e. galaxies with no clear evidence for negative feedback by the AGNs.
ALCS-XAGNs are located on the “simultaneous evolution” line or in the AGN dominant phase, while the other ALMA and *Chandra* selected samples belong to the SF-dominant phase.

We find that our X-ray AGN sample shows both high mass accretion rates (intrinsic 0.5–8 keV X-ray luminosities of ${\sim}10^{\text{44--45}}\,\mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}}$) and star-formation rates (${\gtrsim}100\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$).
showing that a wide and deep survey with ALMA, combined with medium-depth X-ray data, can efficiently detect intense growth stage of both galaxies and SMBHs in high-redshift universe.

This is because infrared radiation from star-formation activity at these redshifts is observed in millimeter band (submillimeter galaxies; SMGs), while X-ray observations can detect the obscured AGNs.
